claims.source: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) contains one of the first discovered and characterized IRESs (Tsukiyama-Kohara et al., 1992) and is the prototype of the structurally similar type 3 viral IRESs, found in some Flaviviridae and Picornaviridae (Hellen and de Breyne, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Tsukiyama-Kohara et al., 1992.

claims.claim: The HCV IRES forms an extended structure containing two major structural domains.
claims.source: The HCV IRES forms an extended structure, containing two major structural domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) (for review: Lukavsky, 2009; Fraser and Doudna, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citations to review articles.

claims.claim: Domain III of the HCV IRES provides affinity for direct binding to the 40S subunit and interactions with eIF3.
claims.source: Domain III (dIII) is the largest and provides the affinity for direct binding to the 40S subunit and interactions with eIF3; it contains multiple stem-loop elements emerging from several junctions.
claims.evidence: This is presented as established knowledge with references to reviews.

claims.claim: Domain II of the HCV IRES is an extended stem-loop that docks on the 40S subunit in the vicinity of the E site.
claims.source: Domain II (dII) is an extended stem-loop that docks on the 40S subunit in the vicinity of the E site.
claims.evidence: This is presented as established knowledge with references to reviews.

claims.claim: The HCV IRES RNA binds directly to the 40S subunit using several IRES structural domains.
claims.source: These studies show that the HCV IRES RNA binds directly to the 40S subunit using several IRES structural domains (Kieft et al., 2001; Lytle et al., 2002, 2001), changing the subunit's conformation (Spahn et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Kieft et al., 2001; Lytle et al., 2002, 2001.

claims.claim: The HCV IRES changes the 40S subunit's conformation upon binding.
claims.source: These studies show that the HCV IRES RNA binds directly to the 40S subunit using several IRES structural domains (Kieft et al., 2001; Lytle et al., 2002, 2001), changing the subunit's conformation (Spahn et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Spahn et al., 2001.

claims.claim: The HCV IRES binds directly to eIF3.
claims.source: The IRES also binds directly to eIF3 (Sizova et al., 1998), which along with the eIF2-containing TC have been described as capable of progressing the HCV IRES preinitiation complex (PIC) to an elongation-competent 80S ribosome (Pestova et al., 1998b).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Sizova et al., 1998.

claims.claim: The HCV IRES can initiate translation when eIF2 is inhibited by phosphorylation of its alpha subunit.
claims.source: In addition, the HCV IRES can also initiate translation when eIF2 is inhibited by phosphorylation of its alpha subunit (Koev et al., 2002; Robert et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Koev et al., 2002; Robert et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Under conditions of eIF2 inhibition, eIF2-independent delivery of Met-tRNAiMet is facilitated by eIF5B.
claims.source: Under these conditions, it is proposed that 40S subunit and eIF3 binding are followed by eIF2-independent delivery of Met-tRNAiMet facilitated by eIF5B (Terenin et al., 2008), or perhaps by less well-understood eIFs 2A or 2D (Dmitriev et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Terenin et al., 2008 as a proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: There is overlap between the binding site of eIF2 and HCV IRES dII on the 40S subunit.
claims.source: Next, recent cryo-EM structures of eukaryotic PICs (Llácer et al., 2015; Quade et al., 2015) show overlap between the binding site of eIF2 (within the TC) and HCV IRES dII on the 40S subunit (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of cryo-EM structures cited from Llácer et al., 2015; Quade et al., 2015, and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claims.claim: HCV actively suppresses eIF2α phosphorylation during infection.
claims.source: Finally, as mentioned above, the HCV IRES has the ability to operate when eIF2 is inactivated by phosphorylation of its alpha subunit, yet during infection HCV actively suppresses eIF2α phosphorylation (Garaigorta and Chisari, 2009; Vyas et al., 2003)
claims.evidence: This is cited from Garaigorta and Chisari, 2009; Vyas et al., 2003.

claims.claim: Translation preinitiation complexes assembled on the HCV IRES contain eIF1A.
claims.source: Translation preinitiation complexes assembled on the HCV IRES contain eIF1A
claims.evidence: This is the title of a results section and is supported by pull-down experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The WT HCV IRES pulled down eIF2, eIF3, and eIF1A, but not eIF1.
claims.source: The WT HCV IRES pulled down eIF2 and eIF3 as expected, and also eIF1A, but not eIF1.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A by western blot analysis.

claims.claim: The CrPV IGR IRES bound 40S subunit but not any initiation factors.
claims.source: Visual examination of the blot shows that as expected, the CrPV IGR IRES bound 40S subunit but not any initiation factors.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A by western blot analysis.

claims.claim: The HCV IRES mutant dIIId_GGG-CCC did not bind 40S subunit, eIF1A, or eIF2 and showed decreased binding of eIF3.
claims.source: A control HCV IRES mutant lacking affinity for the 40S subunit (Kieft et al., 2001), and with severely diminished translation initiation activity (dIIId_GGG-CCC; Figure 1B and C), did not bind 40S subunit, eIF1A, or eIF2 and showed decreased binding of eIF3 (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A by western blot analysis and Figure 1C by translation assays.

claims.claim: Disruption of domain IIIb decreases IRES affinity for eIF3 and translation initiation activity.
claims.source: Disruption of domain IIIb is known to decrease IRES affinity for eIF3 and translation initiation activity (Buratti et al., 1998; Sizova et al., 1998); as expected, mutant dIIIb_trunc decreases the amount of eIF3 pulled down.
claims.evidence: This is cited from Buratti et al., 1998; Sizova et al., 1998 and confirmed by data in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Removing dII or altering its apical loop affects PIC formation and decreases overall translation efficiency.
claims.source: Removing dII (ΔdII) or altering its apical loop (dIIb_ΔGCC) is known to affect PIC formation by changing 40S conformation, inhibiting the proper loading of coding RNA in the decoding groove and decreasing overall translation efficiency (Filbin and Kieft, 2011; Locker et al., 2007; Pestova et al., 2008); as expected they show little or no decrease in bound eIFs 2 and 3.
claims.evidence: This is cited from Filbin and Kieft, 2011; Locker et al., 2007; Pestova et al., 2008 and confirmed by data in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: eIF1A associates with the HCV IRES through the 40S subunit.
claims.source: Overall, these results show that the binding of eIFs depends on IRES binding to the 40S subunit and the effect of these mutations on the binding of eIFs 2 and 3 is consistent with published biochemical studies. Furthermore, these results also suggest that eIF1A is present on these complexes because it associates with the 40S subunit and that the IRES plays some role in its binding stability, suggesting it may be an important functional part of the HCV IRES-assembled PIC.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that eIF1A binding depends on 40S binding and is affected by IRES mutations (Figure 1D, E).

claims.claim: eIF1A's association with HCV IRES PICs does not depend on the presence of RNA in the decoding groove.
claims.source: 3' truncations of the HCV IRES RNA to nucleotide (nt) 344 (3_344; ends after the 'AUG' in the P site), and to nt 330 (3_330; contains no RNA in decoding groove) did not qualitatively change the pattern of factor binding compared to an IRES with 10 codons downstream of the start AUG (3_372) based on a visual examination. This is consistent with eIF1A being recruited through 40S subunit binding to the IRES and not by the protein-coding portion of the IRES RNA.
claims.evidence: This is shown by pull-down experiments with truncated IRES constructs (Figure 1E).

claims.claim: eIF1A associates with the CSFV and SPV-1 IRESs.
claims.source: The presence of eIF1A in HCV IRES PICs led us to test two other type 3 IRESs for eIF1A binding: the aforementioned CSFV IRES and the simian picornavirus type-1 (SPV-1) IRES. eIF1A associates with these IRESs and as with HCV, there is no binding of eIF1 (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is shown by pull-down experiments (Figure 1F).

claims.claim: There is no binding of eIF1 to CSFV and SPV-1 IRESs.
claims.source: eIF1A associates with these IRESs and as with HCV, there is no binding of eIF1 (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is shown by pull-down experiments (Figure 1F).

claims.claim: There are differences in the amount of eIF1A pulled down by different type 3 IRESs.
claims.source: However, a visual inspection reveals interesting differences in the amount of eIF1A pulled down by these IRESs, hinting at differential use of this factor.
claims.evidence: This is observed by visual inspection of western blots in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: eIF1A has been considered dispensable for 48S or 80S complex assembly on type 3 IRESs in the presence of eIF1.
claims.source: Previous studies using reconstituted PIC assembly assays monitored by toeprinting revealed that eIF1A (in the presence of eIF2, 3, and/or 5B) may only moderately enhance the stability of, and is dispensable for, 48S or 80S complex assembly on type 3 IRESs; but, any stabilizing function of eIF1A is completely negated by concurrent addition of eIF1 (Fraser et al., 2009; de Breyne et al., 2008; Pestova et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Fraser et al., 2009; de Breyne et al., 2008; Pestova et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Treatment with α-eIF1A aptamer significantly reduced the amount of eIF1A bound to the HCV IRES without affecting 40S subunit binding.
claims.source: Visual examination of the blot shows that treatment with aptamer did not affect 40S subunit binding to the IRES but significantly reduced the amount of eIF1A bound (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is shown by pull-down experiments with aptamer treatment (Figure 2B).

claims.claim: α-eIF1A aptamer treatment did not affect binding of eIFs 2 and 3 to the HCV IRES.
claims.source: This effect was specific, as binding of eIFs 2 and 3 were not affected, and eIF1 remained unbound (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is shown by pull-down experiments with aptamer treatment (Figure 2B).

claims.claim: Aptamer treatment reduced eIF1A binding on the CSFV and SPV-1 IRESs.
claims.source: Aptamer treatment also reduced eIF1A binding on the CSFV and SPV-1 IRESs, although in the latter case the amount of bound eIF1A is already low, as noted above (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is shown by pull-down experiments with aptamer treatment (Figure 2B).

claims.claim: Treatment of RRL with α-eIF1A decreased translation of a capped reporter.
claims.source: Treatment of RRL (Figure 2E) or HeLa cell lysate (Figure 2F) with α-eIF1A decreased translation of a capped reporter compared to treatment with AS, while CrPV IRES-driven translation either did not change or increased with eIF1A depletion.
claims.evidence: This is shown by translation assays in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: CrPV IRES-driven translation either did not change or increased with eIF1A depletion.
claims.source: Treatment of RRL (Figure 2E) or HeLa cell lysate (Figure 2F) with α-eIF1A decreased translation of a capped reporter compared to treatment with AS, while CrPV IRES-driven translation either did not change or increased with eIF1A depletion.
claims.evidence: This is shown by translation assays in Figure 2E and 2F.

claims.claim: The CrPV IRES is eIF-independent.
claims.source: The behavior of these controls is expected, as cap-dependent translation requires eIF1A, while the CrPV IRES is known to be eIF-independent.
claims.evidence: This is presented as established knowledge.

claims.claim: In RRL, all three type 3 IRESs (HCV, CSFV, SPV-1) showed a decrease in translation with eIF1A depletion.
claims.source: In RRL, all three IRESs showed a decrease in translation with aptamer treatment, with the SPV-1 IRES showing the least and HCV showing the most (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is shown by translation assays in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: In HeLa cell lysate, eIF1A depletion reduced translation initiation by the HCV and CSFV IRESs, but not the SPV-1 IRES.
claims.source: In HeLa cell lysate, eIF1A depletion reduced translation initiation by the HCV and CSFV IRESs, but not the SPV-1 IRES (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This is shown by translation assays in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: In HeLa lysate, the dependence on eIF1A correlates with the amount of eIF1A pulled down.
claims.source: It is noteworthy that in the case of the HeLa lysate, the dependence on eIF1A correlates with the amount of eIF1A pulled down (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is inferred by comparing data from Figure 1F and Figure 2H.

claims.claim: Addition of full-length eIF1A to α-eIF1A-treated RRL restored much of the cap-dependent translation activity.
claims.source: Cap-driven translation and the CrPV IRES controls showed dependence on eIF1A as with monocistronic reporters; adding recombinant full-length eIF1A to the α-eIF1A-treated RRL restored much of the cap-dependent translation activity and returned the CrPV IRES to untreated levels (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is shown by add-back experiments in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Addition of eIF1A lacking the N-terminal tail (ΔNTT) increased cap-dependent translation in the absence of aptamer treatment.
claims.source: Addition of eIF1A lacking the unstructured N-terminal tail (ΔNTT) increased cap-dependent translation in the absence of aptamer treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), perhaps because some mutations to the NTT of eIF1A in yeast exhibit a 'hyper-accurate' phenotype that could support increased translation from a reporter mRNA like the one we use in these studies (Fekete et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and interpreted with reference to Fekete et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Addition of eIF1A with the C-terminal tail deleted (ΔCTT) virtually abolished translation for all initiation mechanisms tested.
claims.source: Addition of eIF1A with the C-terminal tail deleted (ΔCTT) virtually abolished translation for all initiation mechanisms tested (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The diminished HCV IRES activity in eIF1A-depleted lysate was partially restored by add-back of full-length or ΔNTT eIF1A.
claims.source: Applying this approach to translation assays with different type 3 IRESs (Figure 3C), we observed that the diminished HCV IRES activity in eIF1A-depleted lysate was partially restored by add-back of full-length or ΔNTT eIF1A, similar to cap-driven translation.
claims.evidence: This is shown by add-back experiments in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The CSFV IRES did not respond as well to the add-back of full-length eIF1A, but showed more recovery with added ΔNTT eIF1A.
claims.source: The CSFV IRES did not respond as well to the add-back of full-length eIF1A, but showed more recovery with added ΔNTT eIF1A.
claims.evidence: This is shown by add-back experiments in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The SPV-1 IRES was generally less sensitive to eIF1A depletion and add-back of eIF1A had a minimal effect.
claims.source: As noted above, the SPV-1 IRES was generally less sensitive to eIF1A depletion and consistent with this, add-back of eIF1A had a minimal effect.
claims.evidence: This is shown by add-back experiments in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The HCV IRES mutant dIIb_ΔGCC showed some decreased activity with eIF1A depletion but was insensitive to the add-back of eIF1A.
claims.source: The aforementioned dIIb_ ΔGCC mutant (activity is ~40% of WT, Figure 1C) is defective in docking coding RNA into the decoding groove (Filbin and Kieft, 2011); it showed some decreased activity with eIF1A depletion but was insensitive to the add-back of eIF1A.
claims.evidence: This is shown by add-back experiments in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: eIF1A's role involves positioning or recognizing RNA in the decoding groove.
claims.source: This preliminarily suggests that eIF1A's role involves positioning or recognizing RNA in the decoding groove.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the behavior of the dIIb_ΔGCC mutant which is defective in docking coding RNA and is insensitive to eIF1A add-back.

claims.claim: The HCV IRES AUG-CUG mutant's activity was enhanced by the depletion of eIF1A.
claims.source: Interestingly, this mutant's activity was enhanced by the depletion of eIF1A but then decreased with add-back of either full-length eIF1A or the ΔNTT mutant (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is shown by add-back experiments in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: eIF1A function on the HCV IRES involves recognition of RNA in the decoding groove, likely inspecting the AUG codon and its pairing with the anticodon of Met-tRNAiMet.
claims.source: Overall, these data suggest that eIF1A function on the HCV IRES (and other type 3 IRESs) involves recognition of RNA in the decoding groove, likely inspecting the AUG codon and its pairing with the anticodon of Met-tRNAiMet.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the behavior of the AUG-CUG mutant and the dIIb_ΔGCC mutant in eIF1A depletion and add-back experiments (Figure 3C).

claims.claim: PICs from unstressed 293F cells contain eIFs 3, 2, and 1A but little or no 5B.
claims.source: PICs from unstressed 293F cells without added IRES contain eIFs 3, 2, and 1A but little or no 5B, as expected (Figure 4A, lane 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: PICs from stressed cells showed a similar pattern to unstressed cells but with dramatic reduction in bound eIF2.
claims.source: PICs from stressed cells showed a similar pattern but with dramatic reduction in bound eIF2 (Figure 4B, lane 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: There was no phosphorylated eIF2α bound to PICs from stressed cells.
claims.source: There was no phosphorylated eIF2α bound, as expected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Adding WT HCV IRES to purified preassembled PICs displaced eIF2, while eIF3 and eIF1A remained bound.
claims.source: Adding WT HCV IRES to the purified preassembled PICs had similar effects on PICs from both stressed and unstressed cells. Specifically, eIF2 was displaced, while eIF3 and eIF1A remained bound (Figure 4A and B, lanes 2 and 8).
claims.evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Both eIF1A and eIF5B showed increased binding or retention when the HCV IRES was present.
claims.source: Both eIF1A and eIF5B showed increased binding or retention when the HCV IRES was present, more obviously with PICs from stressed cells.
claims.evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: There was more eIF5B present overall in complexes from stressed cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, there was more eIF5B present overall in complexes from stressed cells.
claims.evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Addition of HCV IRES to pre-formed 43S complexes results in PICs capable of progressing to 80S ribosomes.
claims.source: If we use eIF5B's presence as a proxy for a 48S complex prepared to progress to 80S ribosomes, these results suggest: (1) addition of HCV IRES to pre-formed 43S complexes results in PICs capable of progressing to 80S ribosomes
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the presence of eIF5B on HCV IRES-bound PICs (Figure 4A and B).

claims.claim: Under stress, the relevant HCV IRES complex can form without eIF2 but contains eIFs 3, 5B, and 1A.
claims.source: and (2) under stress, the relevant HCV IRES complex can form without eIF2 but contains eIFs 3, 5B, and 1A.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the composition of PICs from stressed cells bound to HCV IRES (Figure 4B).

claims.claim: GMP-PNP exchange was effective enough to prevent 80S ribosome formation on both capped β-globin mRNAs and HCV IRES RNAs.
claims.source: GMP-PNP exchange was effective enough to prevent 80S ribosome formation on both capped β-globin mRNAs and HCV IRES RNAs (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is shown by sucrose gradient analysis in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Purified PICs from GMP-PNP-treated lysate contained eIFs 3, 2, and 1A but no eIF1.
claims.source: Purified PICs from GMP-PNP-treated lysate contained eIFs 3, 2, and 1A but again no eIF1.
claims.evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Addition of HCV IRES to GMP-PNP-treated PICs resulted in retention of eIFs 3 and 1A, but there was little or no bound eIF5B.
claims.source: Addition of HCV IRES resulted in retention of eIFs 3 and 1A, but there was little or no bound eIF5B on these HCV PICs, as expected (Figure 4D, lanes 2 and 8).
claims.evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: eIF2 was displaced from GMP-PNP-treated PICs by the HCV IRES.
claims.source: eIF2 was again displaced from these PICs by the IRES.
claims.evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Altering dIIIb (dIIIb_trunc) had a small effect on eIF3 in the complex despite the fact that mutation of this domain dramatically reduces direct eIF3 binding to the HCV and CSFV IRESs.
claims.source: Altering dIIIb (dIIIb_trunc) had a small effect on eIF3 in the complex despite the fact that mutation of this domain dramatically reduces direct eIF3 binding to the HCV and CSFV IRESs (Figure 4A,B and D, lanes 3 and 9) (Kieft et al., 2001; Sizova et al., 1998), again consistent with a mechanism in which eIF3 is recruited by interactions with the 40S subunit.
claims.evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 4A, B, and D, and cited from Kieft et al., 2001; Sizova et al., 1998.

claims.claim: A PIC with dIIIb_trunc did not contain eIF5B.
claims.source: However, a PIC with dIIIb_trunc did not contain eIF5B, which would inhibit progression to 80S ribosomes.
claims.evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 4A, B, and D.

claims.claim: Removal of dII (ΔdII) slightly decreased 40S-bound eIF1A but increased retained eIF2.
claims.source: Removal of dII (ΔdII) slightly decreased 40S-bound eIF1A but increased retained eIF2 (Figure 4A, lanes 4 and 10), again consistent with a potential clash between dII and eIF2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 4A and interpreted with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claims.claim: With PICs from stressed cells with ΔdII mutant, there is no eIF2 binding and eIF1A is less well retained.
claims.source: With PICs from stressed cells with this mutant, there is no eIF2 binding (as expected) and eIF1A is less well retained (Figure 4B, lanes 4 and 10)
claims.evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: IRES dII helps keep eIF1A bound.
claims.source: Hence, IRES dII may somewhat compete for eIF2 binding (in a position docked in the E site), but it helps keep eIF1A bound.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the behavior of the ΔdII mutant in PIC remodeling experiments (Figure 4A and B).

claims.claim: The ΔdII mutant does not recover activity when cells are stressed.
claims.source: An interesting consequence of dII deletion is that the mutant does not recover activity when cells are stressed (Figure 4E), perhaps due to the decreased binding of eIF1A.
claims.evidence: This is shown by translation assays in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: With PICs from unstressed cells, dIIb_ΔGCC did not cause as much dissociation of eIF2.
claims.source: With PICs from unstressed cells, dIIb_ΔGCC did not cause as much dissociation of eIF2 (Figure 4A, lanes 5 and 11), consistent with cryo-EM reconstructions of this mutant which show an altered location of dII (Filbin et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 4A and cited from Filbin et al., 2013.

claims.claim: dIIb_ΔGCC has inhibited translation initiation in unstressed cells, but more than recovered activity in stressed cells.
claims.source: This correlates with a dramatic increase in activity with stress: dIIb_ΔGCC has inhibited translation initiation in unstressed cells, but more than recovered activity in stressed cells (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is shown by translation assays in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: With AUG-CUG, eIF1A was bound under all conditions, and eIF1 was retained with PICs from unstressed cells and to a certain degree on GMP-PNP-treated PICs.
claims.source: With AUG-CUG, eIF1A was bound under all conditions, and eIF1 was retained with PICs from unstressed cells and to a certain degree on GMP-PNP-treated PICs (Figure 4A and D, lanes 6 and 12).
claims.evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 4A and D.

claims.claim: AUG-CUG induces only a 50% decrease in activity in unstressed cells, but its activity is decreased dramatically when the cells are stressed.
claims.source: Interestingly, AUG-CUG induces only a 50% decrease in activity in unstressed cells, but strikingly its activity is decreased dramatically when the cells are stressed, dropping to levels similar to the negative control mutant dIIId_GGG-CCC (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is shown by translation assays in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The HCV IRES's AUG start codon is much more important for function when eIF2 is depleted.
claims.source: Thus, the HCV IRES's AUG start codon is much more important for function when eIF2 is depleted.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the behavior of the AUG-CUG mutant in stressed versus unstressed cells (Figure 4E).

claims.claim: eIF5B binding to PICs from DTT-treated cells is higher when eIFs 2 and 1 are absent and 1A and 3 are present.
claims.source: Overall, eIF5B binding to PICs from DTT-treated cells is higher when eIFs 2 and 1 are absent and 1A and 3 are present.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of eIF5B binding across different conditions in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: α-eIF1A aptamer treatment has no effect on eIF2 binding in unstressed or DTT-stressed PICs bound with WT HCV IRES.
claims.source: First, using PICs purified from both unstressed and DTT-stressed cells, we verified that aptamer treatment does not positively or negatively affect binding of eIF2 (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: In the absence of aptamer or IRES, eIF2-bound PICs contain more tRNAi than do PICs from DTT-treated cells.
claims.source: In the absence of aptamer or IRES, eIF2-bound PICs contain more tRNAi (assessed relative to 18S rRNA) than do PICs from DTT-treated cells, although the latter retain tRNAi above background levels, indicating some stably bound tRNAi to these purified PICs without eIF2.
claims.evidence: This is shown by Northern blot analysis in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Under conditions of eIF2 abundance, treatment with the α-eIF1A aptamer and IRES binding induced no reproducibly statistically significant change in tRNAi binding.
claims.source: Under conditions of eIF2 abundance, treatment with the α-eIF1A aptamer and IRES binding induced no reproducibly statistically significant change in tRNAi binding (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is shown by Northern blot analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: When PICs from stressed cells were treated with α-eIF1A aptamer, it reduced the amount of tRNAi bound to WT HCV IRES-containing PICs.
claims.source: However, when we repeated this analysis with PICs from stressed cells, treatment with α-eIF1A aptamer reduced the amount of tRNAi bound to WT HCV IRES-containing PICs (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is shown by Northern blot analysis in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Binding of the AUG-CUG mutant to PICs from stressed cells decreased tRNAi binding, but depletion of eIF1A increased tRNAi binding.
claims.source: Binding of the AUG-CUG mutant to PICs from stressed cells also decreased tRNAi binding, but depletion of eIF1A increased tRNAi binding.
claims.evidence: This is shown by Northern blot analysis in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: In the context of HCV IRES translation, eIF1A contributes to stable tRNAi binding but is also involved in discriminating against non-AUG start codons, and this role is particularly important during stress conditions.
claims.source: Taken together, these data suggest that in the context of HCV IRES translation, eIF1A is performing roles analogous to its canonical roles: it contributes to stable tRNAi binding but is also involved in discriminating against non-AUG start codons, and this role is particularly important during stress conditions.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the tRNAi binding experiments with eIF1A depletion and the AUG-CUG mutant (Figure 5C).

claims.claim: eIF1A depletion and resultant tRNAi binding does not correlate with the presence of eIF5B on complexes.
claims.source: Furthermore, eIF1A depletion and resultant tRNAi binding does not correlate with the presence of eIF5B on complexes (Figure 5D, compare to Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is inferred by comparing data from Figure 5D and Figure 4.

claims.claim: eIF5B and eIF1A are very likely acting as partners in post-tRNAi binding subunit association.
claims.source: Hence, eIF5B and eIF1A are very likely acting as partners in post-tRNAi binding subunit association, and while eIF5B is playing an important role in tRNAi binding and subunit joining, it is not likely acting as a direct tRNAi delivery agent when eIF2 is depleted.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between eIF5B presence and tRNAi binding upon eIF1A depletion.

results.result: Translation preinitiation complexes (PICs) assembled on the HCV IRES contain eIF1A but not eIF1. Pull-down experiments show that the WT HCV IRES binds eIF2, eIF3, and eIF1A, but not eIF1. Similar results were observed for CSFV and SPV-1 IRESs, with differences in the amount of eIF1A pulled down by different type 3 IRESs.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C22, C25, C27-C29 are supported by pull-down experiments with biotinylated IRES RNAs and western blot analysis (Figure 1A, 1D-F). The specificity is demonstrated by appropriate controls (CrPV IRES, mutant HCV IRES). The observation that eIF1A associates through the 40S subunit is supported by the dependence of eIF1A binding on 40S binding and the effects of IRES mutations.

results.result: eIF1A is necessary for efficient HCV IRES activity. Depletion of eIF1A using an RNA aptamer reduced translation from HCV, CSFV, and SPV-1 IRESs in both RRL and HeLa lysate, with varying degrees of dependence. The aptamer specifically depleted eIF1A without affecting eIF2 or eIF3 binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C32-C36, C38-C40 are supported by aptamer depletion experiments (Figure 2B-H) showing reduced translation activity upon eIF1A depletion. The specificity of the aptamer is demonstrated by controls showing no effect on eIF2/eIF3 binding and expected effects on cap-dependent and CrPV IRES translation. Statistical significance is reported for translation assays.

results.result: Add-back of recombinant eIF1A to depleted lysate partially restored HCV IRES activity. The C-terminal tail (CTT) of eIF1A is essential for translation, while the N-terminal tail (NTT) modulates activity. The AUG-CUG start codon mutant showed enhanced activity upon eIF1A depletion, suggesting eIF1A inspects the AUG codon and its pairing with Met-tRNAiMet.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C50 are supported by add-back experiments (Figure 3B-C) showing partial restoration of translation activity with full-length and ΔNTT eIF1A, and complete inhibition with ΔCTT. The behavior of the AUG-CUG mutant (enhanced activity upon eIF1A depletion, decreased with add-back) supports the role of eIF1A in codon inspection. The dIIb_ΔGCC mutant's insensitivity to eIF1A add-back supports a role in decoding groove recognition.

results.result: The HCV IRES binds and remodels preassembled PICs. Addition of HCV IRES to natively purified PICs from unstressed or DTT-stressed cells displaced eIF2 while retaining eIF3 and eIF1A. eIF5B binding increased, especially in stressed cells, suggesting formation of complexes capable of progressing to 80S ribosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C51-C58 are supported by experiments with natively purified PICs (Figure 4A-B). Western blot analysis shows the composition of PICs before and after IRES binding, demonstrating eIF2 displacement and eIF1A/eIF3 retention. The presence of eIF5B is used as a proxy for 48S complex formation, though this inference is reasonable but not directly proven. The approach is validated by appropriate controls.

results.result: GMP-PNP treatment prevented 80S ribosome formation and affected PIC composition. PICs from GMP-PNP-treated lysate contained eIFs 3, 2, and 1A. Addition of HCV IRES displaced eIF2 and retained eIF3 and eIF1A, but little or no eIF5B was bound.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 are supported by sucrose gradient analysis (Figure 4C) showing prevention of 80S formation, and western blot analysis (Figure 4D) showing PIC composition. The effectiveness of GMP-PNP exchange is demonstrated. The absence of eIF5B on these complexes is expected given the role of GTP hydrolysis in subunit joining.

results.result: Different HCV IRES structural domains contribute to PIC remodeling and translation activity. Domain IIIb affects eIF5B binding, domain II affects eIF1A retention and eIF2 displacement, and the AUG start codon is more important under stress conditions. The dIIb_ΔGCC mutant shows increased activity under stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C74 are supported by experiments with HCV IRES mutants (Figure 4A-E) showing differential effects on factor binding and translation activity under stressed and unstressed conditions. The correlation between factor binding and translation activity is demonstrated. The increased sensitivity of the AUG-CUG mutant to stress is shown by translation assays with statistical significance.

results.result: eIF1A stabilizes tRNAi binding to HCV IRES PICs, especially under stress conditions. In PICs from stressed cells, eIF1A depletion reduced tRNAi binding to WT HCV IRES. The AUG-CUG mutant showed decreased tRNAi binding, but eIF1A depletion increased it, suggesting eIF1A discriminates against non-AUG codons.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C75-C80 are supported by Northern blot experiments measuring tRNAi binding (Figure 5A-C). The specificity is demonstrated by showing no effect of aptamer on eIF2 binding. The differential effects under stressed versus unstressed conditions and with the AUG-CUG mutant support the proposed roles of eIF1A. Statistical significance is reported for key comparisons.

results.result: eIF1A and eIF5B likely act as partners in post-tRNAi binding subunit association. eIF1A depletion and resultant tRNAi binding does not correlate with eIF5B presence on complexes, suggesting eIF5B is not acting as a direct tRNAi delivery agent when eIF2 is depleted.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 are supported by comparing data from Figure 5D and Figure 4, showing lack of correlation between eIF5B presence and tRNAi binding upon eIF1A depletion. This inference is reasonable given the data, though the mechanism of tRNAi delivery in the absence of eIF2 is not directly demonstrated.

results.result: eIF2A and eIF2D are not substituting for eIF2 during HCV IRES-driven translation under stress. Knockdown of eIF2A and/or eIF2D did not affect HCV IRES function under stress, while partial knockdown of eIF1A decreased HCV IRES translation.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by siRNA knockdown experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) showing no effect of eIF2A/2D depletion on HCV IRES translation under stress, while eIF1A knockdown decreased translation. The knockdown efficiency is demonstrated by western blot. This result contradicts some prior proposals in the literature but is supported by the data presented.

results.result: The HCV IRES remodels PICs to generate initiation complexes with bacterial-like features. eIF1A performs roles analogous to its canonical functions: stabilizing tRNAi binding, discriminating against improper codons, and stimulating eIF5B-mediated subunit joining. The IRES may promote a 'closed-like' conformation that stabilizes eIF1A binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C86-C92 are supported by the collective data from translation assays, tRNAi binding experiments, and add-back experiments with eIF1A mutants. The functional similarities to canonical initiation and bacterial initiation are supported by cited literature. The proposed model of a 'closed-like' conformation is inferred from structural data and functional observations, though not directly proven.

results.result: The authors propose a mechanistic model in which the HCV IRES recruits a pre-assembled 'TC-deficient' PIC containing eIFs 1, 1A, and 3. The IRES remodels this PIC by displacing eIF1 and partially displacing eIF3. Under stress, increased levels of TC-deficient PICs would be available for IRES binding. Met-tRNAiMet binding can occur directly or via the TC, with eIF1A and eIF5B working together for final stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C105 represent the proposed mechanistic model, which is supported by the collective experimental data presented in the manuscript. The model is consistent with the observation that natively purified PICs contain eIFs 1A, 2, and 3 (C96), the IRES displaces eIF2 and eIF1 while retaining eIF1A and eIF3 (C54, C100), and the increased activity under stress (C70, C72). The model integrates prior knowledge with new findings, though some aspects remain speculative.

results.result: The proposed mechanism shares features with bacterial translation initiation. eIF1A is the functional homolog of bacterial IF1, and the combination of eIF1A, 5B, and 3 parallels IFs 1, 2, and 3. Direct Met-tRNAiMet binding is supported by prior studies and the increased sensitivity of the AUG-CUG mutant to stress. Stress granules contain TC-deficient PICs, supporting the model.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C118 are supported by cited literature and the data presented in this manuscript. The functional similarities between eIF1A and IF1 are supported by cited studies (C115). The increased sensitivity of the AUG-CUG mutant to stress (C110) supports the idea that direct tRNAi binding is more dependent on codon-anticodon interaction. The presence of TC-deficient PICs in stress granules (C106) is cited from prior work and supports the proposed model.

results.result: Background and prior work on HCV IRES structure, function, and translation initiation mechanisms. The HCV IRES is the prototype for type 3 IRESs, contains two major structural domains, binds directly to the 40S subunit and eIF3, and can function when eIF2 is inhibited. Prior studies suggested eIF1A was dispensable for type 3 IRES function.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C18, C23-C24, C30, C37, C93-C95 represent background knowledge and prior work, supported by appropriate citations. These claims establish the context for the current study and are generally accepted in the field. The structural information is supported by cited reviews and structural studies. The functional information is supported by cited biochemical studies.

results.result: eIF1A's association with HCV IRES PICs does not depend on the presence of RNA in the decoding groove, and natively purified PICs have eIFs preloaded. Truncation experiments show similar factor binding patterns regardless of coding RNA presence.
results.evaluation: Claims C26 and C96 are supported by pull-down experiments with truncated IRES constructs (Figure 1E) and western blot analysis of purified PICs (Figure 4A, B, D). The observation that factor binding is similar with different 3' truncations supports the conclusion that eIF1A is recruited through 40S binding rather than by the coding RNA.

results.result: eIF1A inspects the codon-anticodon interaction during HCV IRES-driven translation, involving recognition of RNA in the decoding groove and inspection of the AUG codon and its pairing with Met-tRNAiMet.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C48, C50 are supported by experiments with the AUG-CUG mutant (Figure 3C, 4E, 5C) showing that eIF1A depletion increases translation of this mutant, and the dIIb_ΔGCC mutant showing insensitivity to eIF1A add-back. These observations support the proposed role of eIF1A in codon inspection, though the molecular mechanism is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.
